# Five years of app evaluation: Insights from a framework in practice – a systematic review on the m-health index and navigation database

**Authors:** Julian Herpertz; Bridget Dwyer; Ellen Wagner; Jane Mikkelson; Nils Opel; John Torous

**Affiliations:** aCharite – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, Campus Benjamin Franklin, Berlin, Germany | bDivision of Digital Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | cHarvard T.H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | dGerman Center for Mental Health (DZPG), partner site Berlin-Potsdam, Germany

## Abstract

As the number of health apps continues to rise, concerns about their quality, privacy standards, and adherence to evidence-based healthcare remain. While multiple frameworks exist to assess app quality, a standardized, cross-domain approach is lacking. The M-Health Index and Navigation Database (MIND) comprises a structured framework for app evaluation and a publicly accessible database that applies this framework to rate individual apps. This allows for longitudinal tracking of quality metrics and comparisons across different health app categories.

We conducted a systematic review to identify studies that utilized either the MIND database or its framework to evaluate health apps. Studies were included if they used MIND in their methodology to evaluate health apps. Data were synthesized descriptively, and two-proportion z-tests were applied for comparisons.

We identified 22 studies, including 16 evaluating commercially available health apps. The most frequently assessed metrics were privacy policies, operating system compatibility, cost, and evidence backing. Only 15 % of mental health apps were supported by feasibility or efficacy studies, nearly one-fourth lacked a privacy policy, and 44 % explicitly disclosed sharing personal health information with third parties. Similar deficiencies were found across non-mental health domains, indicating that concerns regarding app quality and data privacy may not be unique to mental health.

Our findings suggest that evidence and privacy concerns are prevalent across almost all health app categories, highlighting the need for stronger regulatory oversight and improved validation standards. MIND serves as a valuable tool for evaluating digital health apps, supporting both app selection and cross-domain quality comparisons.

Keywords: App evaluation, Information management, Mobile health apps, Telemedicine, Mental health apps, Digital interventions, Evaluation framework

## Abstract

The MIND database is a valuable tool for assessing app quality, enabling longitudinal tracking and cross-domain comparisons.

Only 15% of general mental health apps had feasibility or efficacy data. Apps in other health domains showed similarly low evidence.

Nearly one-fourth of mental health apps lacked a privacy policy. Smoking cessation apps had lower rates of available policies.

Nearly half of mental health apps shared PHI; pneumology and COVID-19 apps had lower, and cardiovascular apps had higher rates.

The quality issues observed in mental health apps are not unique but reflective of wider concerns across healthcare domains.

## Introduction

The growing demand for health services, coupled with a persistent shortage of trained professionals (Stringer, 2024), has driven the exploration of scalable solutions to bridge this gap in healthcare. Among these solutions, mobile health applications (mHealth apps) have garnered significant attention as tools claiming to democratize health care access (Giebel et al., 2024). Their marketing often portrays them as transformative and capable of bridging the gap in health-care accessibility, especially for underserved populations. However, a closer examination reveals that evidence does not often substantiate these promises (Huckvale et al., 2019; Bae et al., 2023).

While mHealth apps are theoretically well-positioned to reduce barriers to care and complement traditional therapeutic approaches (Torous et al., 2021), significant concerns undermine their widespread adoption. The first challenge is the sheer number of available health apps - over 300,000 globally (Bates et al., 2018) - which creates an overwhelming and fragmented marketplace (Torous and Roberts, 2017). For both clinicians and patients, identifying a suitable app can be challenging, akin to finding a needle in a haystack (Psihogios et al., 2020). Without proper guidance, users often resort to trial-and-error, which risks delaying care or causing harm (Camacho et al., 2022a). The second challenge is the vast discrepancy in app quality. Apps vary significantly in their clinical validity, usability, data security, and adherence to evidence-based practices (Torous et al., 2018a). Many apps make unsubstantiated claims of efficacy, fail to protect data, or employ outdated or incorrect therapeutic principles (Torous et al., 2023).

Recognizing the need for standardized quality assessment, numerous frameworks for evaluating health apps have been proposed. Defined as criteria-based tools for assessing the quality of mobile health apps (Ramos et al., 2021), a recent review identified more than 100 distinct frameworks, each varying in evaluation methodologies and quality criteria (Frey et al., 2023). This abundance of frameworks creates significant challenges in comparing app quality across studies, as inconsistent evaluation criteria hinder the ability to draw meaningful conclusions.

A notable example of an app evaluation framework is the model developed by the American Psychiatric Association (APA), which outlines five key criteria for app assessment: Access and Background, Privacy and Security, Clinical Foundation, Usability, and Data Integration toward Therapeutic Goals (App Advisor An American Psychiatric Association Initiative, n.d.; Henson et al., 2019). While the APA framework is a valuable tool, its practical application presents challenges. Clinicians and patients often lack the time and expertise to thoroughly investigate each app against these criteria. The complexity of evaluating apps on dimensions like clinical effectiveness or data security can be overwhelming, particularly for users without technical backgrounds. Recognizing this gap, the APA framework has been translated into a dynamic and user-friendly database: the M-Health Index and Navigation Database (MIND; mindapps.org).

MIND builds on the APA's evaluation framework by translating its principles into a structured, operational framework consisting of 105 standardized yes/no quality indicators. These indicators make the APA criteria practically applicable and allow for consistent app evaluation across domains. Trained raters use the MIND framework to assess each app across key dimensions such as clinical foundation, data privacy, and user engagement (Fig. 1). After being rated by the MIND app rater team, apps are added to the MIND database. Each app then undergoes a review and update at least every six months ensuring that the apps remain functional, and their ratings are revised to reflect any changes or updates. Five years after its development, there are now more than 500 apps presented on the platform and the spectrum of apps has broadened: while initially developed to transparently evaluate mental health apps, the platform now also encompasses health apps in the field of neurology and cardiology.

MIND helps bridge the gap between theoretical evaluation frameworks and practical decision-making, empowering users with tailored recommendations that align with their needs. However, the value of MIND extends beyond app recommendations. The database is a resource for research, offering insights into trends in app development, usage, and evaluation (database adoption). Moreover, the evaluation process is transparent to the public so that the framework's methodology can be applied to any other app not registered in the database (framework adoption). By using a unified evaluation methodology that underlies both the MIND database and independent applications of the MIND framework, it has become possible to compare app quality reliably across sources. Findings from different areas of research and healthcare can be meaningfully aligned, enabling the assessment of app quality trends and developments over recent years.

MIND has been utilized in numerous studies evaluating the quality of general mental health apps, establishing its standards as a benchmark for comparison (Camacho et al., 2022a; Stoeckl et al., 2023; Funnell et al., 2022; Lagan et al., 2021a) The most recent study found that only 15 % of over 500 analyzed apps included a feasibility or efficacy study. Furthermore, while approximately three-quarters of the apps had a privacy policy, nearly half of these policies disclosed that user data was shared with third-party companies (Camacho et al., 2022a). Small effect sizes and questionable privacy standards are well-documented concerns in the domain of mental health apps (Linardon et al., 2024; Iwaya et al., 2023). However, whether these issues are unique to mental health applications or represent a broader challenge across the entire health app landscape remains unclear. This systematic review aims to compare findings on evaluation metrics of general mental health apps with those of non-mental health apps and apps for specific mental health disorders to determine whether observed issues are specific to the mental health domain or reflective of broader trends in the health app landscape.

We aim to demonstrate the utility of MIND as a resource for researchers exploring the evolving field of digital health. Highlighting its applications in diverse areas such as personalized patient care, app evaluation, and policy development, this review seeks to inspire broader use of MIND in research and encourage investigators to leverage its potential for generating new insights.

## Methodology

This review was conducted according to the protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42024629259).

### Identification of articles

The systematic search followed the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Literature searches were conducted in Google Scholar, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, focusing on identifying peer-reviewed articles that used the MIND framework or database in their methodology. Articles published between January 1, 2019, and December 18, 2024, were included in the search (Table 1). A detailed search strategy is provided in the supplementary materials.

The study selection process consisted of two steps. First, one reviewer screened titles and abstracts to identify articles that met the inclusion criteria. Eligible articles were then subjected to a full-text review by two reviewers. Any discrepancies in the final list of included articles were resolved through discussion.

### Analyzing evaluation metrics across time and health domains

We assessed the proportion of apps that met evaluation metrics, including whether an app was backed by feasibility or efficacy studies (evidence), whether it was developed by a for-profit company, whether it shared personal health information (PHI) with third parties, whether users had access to its privacy policies, and whether it was entirely free to use, meaning no payments, in-app purchases, or subscriptions were required. Additionally, we considered key functional features: whether apps provided accessibility options, such as adjustable text size, text-to-speech or speech-to-text capabilities, colorblind-friendly display settings, offline functionalities and data export capabilities.

To assess whether the proportion of mental health apps meeting each evaluation metric changed significantly over time through updates or other implemented changes, we conducted two-proportion z-tests for each consecutive pair of years. Similarly, we compared findings on non-mental health apps and apps targeting specific mental health disorders with general mental health apps, using the most recent available data on general mental health apps as the reference category.

## Results

### Identification of articles

We identified 22 articles that met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis of this review (Fig. 2). Please refer to the supplementary material to get an overview of all included studies.

*Fig. 2: Prisma diagram of articles included in this review.*

Twelve of the 22 (55 %) included articles were authored either by the MIND developers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center or in collaboration with them. Nineteen articles utilized either the MIND framework or the database to evaluate the quality of health apps. The remaining three studies pursued different research approaches: one study developed a questionnaire, subsequently uploaded to the database, to explore app engagement among MIND users (Kopka et al., 2023). Another study examined whether a digital phenotyping approach could improve engagement with four mental health apps originally identified through MIND (Dwyer et al., 2024). Lastly, Quach et al (Quach et al., 2024). used the MIND framework to create a questionnaire aimed at identifying desired features for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) applications to support self-management for patients and healthcare professionals.

Of the 19 articles that used MIND to investigate the quality of health apps, ten (53 %) based their evaluations on data extracted directly from the MIND database, while nine (47 %) applied the MIND framework independently to assess apps not listed in the database. Sixteen of the 19 studies that conducted an app quality assessment utilized MIND to evaluate apps available on either the Apple App Store or Google Play Store. Two studies explored alternative resources to identify smartphone applications, conducting systematic reviews of the research literature to identify controlled studies that evaluated the quality of health apps for cancer care (Donkor et al., 2023) or chronic lung diseases (Quach et al., 2023a) using the MIND framework. Many of the apps investigated in these studies were developed by research teams and were not publicly accessible. Notably, one of three studies focused not on apps designed for patients but rather on those aimed at assisting clinicians in decision-making across the spectrum of coronary artery disease (Grubman et al., 2023).

The sixteen studies assessed various categories of health apps: four studies (22 %) focused on general mental health apps, while the remaining studies addressed a range of health domains, including perinatal mental health (11 %, n = 2), pneumological diseases (11 %, n = 2), cardiovascular health (11 %, n = 2) and single studies (5 % each) on smoking cessation, eating disorders, cancer, COVID-19, temporomandibular disorders, trauma, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and neurology (Fig. 2).

The eleven most frequently assessed evaluation metrics across the sixteen studies, in descending order, were: the presence of a privacy policy, operating system compatibility, the proportion of completely free apps, how many apps were supported by studies, user data exportability, sharing of PHI, availability of offline functionality, inclusion of mindfulness and journaling features, development by for-profit companies, and the presence of accessibility features.

### Analyzing evaluation metrics across time and health domains

The studies which assessed evaluation metrics of mental health apps used the MIND database over three consecutive years (2021, 2022, and 2023). During this period, the number of apps providing access to a privacy policy significantly decreased from 238 of 278 (86 %) apps to 443 of 578 (77 %) apps (z = 3.507, p = .002), while the proportion of apps developed by for-profit companies significantly increased from 76 % to 88 % (z = −3.716, p < .001; Table 2). There was a significant decline in the number of completely free-to-use apps (z = 7.654, p < .001) and apps that allowed users to export their usage data (z = 3.268, p = .001). Between 2021 and 2022, there was no significant change in the proportion of mental health apps backed by evidence (z = 0.429, p = .628), nor in the proportion of apps sharing PHI (z = −1.555, p = .120; Table 2).

In the most recent investigation, 85 of 578 (15 %) mental health apps were supported by feasibility or efficacy studies, a significantly higher proportion compared to apps designed for smoking cessation (z = 3.028, p = .002; Fig. 3), and cardiovascular care apps (z = −2.028, p = .043). The majority of apps designed to provide guidance for individuals diagnosed with bipolar disorder were supported by feasibility or efficacy studies. However, only nine apps were included in the investigation of evaluation metrics for bipolar disorder apps.

*Fig. 3: Comparison of the Proportion of Apps Meeting the Top Five Evaluation Criteria Across Health Domains. R: Mental health apps serve as the reference category for two-proportion z-tests. Only studies investigating apps accessible on the Apple App or Google Play Stores were included in this analysis.*

Regarding data privacy, 443 of 578 (77 %) mental health apps provided access to a privacy policy. Most app categories did not differ significantly from mental health apps in this regard, with the exception of smoking cessation apps and neurology apps. Only 108 of 180 (60 %) smoking cessation apps offered a privacy policy, a significantly lower proportion (z = 4.376, p < .001), whereas 177 of 201 (88 %) neurology apps had a privacy policy, a significantly higher proportion (z = 3.459, p < .001). Overall, a substantial proportion of apps across all categories shared personal health information with third-party companies, including 257 of 578 (44 %) investigated mental health apps. Apps designed for pneumological conditions (z = 2.090, p = .037) and schizophrenia (z = 3.085, p = .002) were significantly less likely to share PHI, although only six and 13 apps, respectively, were included in those studies. In contrast, cardiovascular care apps were significantly more likely to share PHI (z = −2.410, p = .016).

In the most recent study, 172 of 578 (30 %) mental health apps provided users with the option to export and share their data. This feature was significantly more common in cardiovascular care (z = 7.252, p < .001), trauma (z = 2.048, p = .040), and bipolar disorder apps (z = 3.818, p < .001; Fig. 3). General mental health apps had a comparatively high proportion of accessibility features, with all other app categories, except for bipolar disorder apps (67 %, z = −0.758, p = .448), offering significantly fewer accessibility features. The majority of apps across nearly all categories were capable of functioning offline. Smoking cessation apps had a significantly higher proportion of offline functionalities compared to general mental health apps (z = −4.131, p < .001), with 147 of 180 (82 %) investigated apps supporting offline use. In contrast, eating disorder apps were significantly less likely to function independently of an internet connection (z = 3.296, p < .001; Table 2).

## Discussion

A standardized approach to evaluating health apps across all medical fields has been a longstanding goal, driven by the need for consistent quality assessments, transparency, and evidence-based recommendations (Camacho et al., 2020; Lagan et al., 2020). MIND has been shown to support the majority of quality assessments in digital health, making it suitable tool for measuring longitudinal changes in and comparing health apps across different medical categories (Lagan et al., 2021b). The finding that nearly half of the included studies applied MIND's framework to a completely new app category not yet included in the database demonstrates its widespread adoption and versatility across different app categories. Our findings confirm that major issues in the field of health apps, such as a lack of supporting evidence and, in some cases, missing or often questionable privacy policies, are not exclusive to mental health applications but extend across various medical domains. While individual studies included in our analysis highlighted deficiencies in app quality within specific domains, our comparative overview suggests that such issues may not be unique to mental health but could also be present in other areas of digital health.

We found that the presence of privacy policies, the proportion of completely free apps, operating system compatibility (Android/iOS), evidence assessment, data export functionality, and the sharing of personal health information are the most important evaluation metrics for researchers in this field. Future studies assessing the quality of new health app categories should consider these metrics to ensure comparability with our established standards.

The declining number of mental health apps providing access to privacy policies is concerning, as recent literature suggests that the absence of a privacy policy indicates that an app follows questionable standards regarding data protection (Torous et al., 2018b). Other app categories, with the exception of neurology apps, do not perform better in this regard. Providing users with clear information on how their personal data is handled should be considered a minimum quality standard for all health apps. While researchers have repeatedly emphasized this issue within the mental health domain (Parker et al., 2019; Melcher et al., 2022; Koh et al., 2022), similar deficiencies in other health app categories have not yet received the same level of attention.

The mere existence of a privacy policy does not guarantee responsible handling of user data. Nearly half of all mental health apps explicitly state in their policies that they share PHI with third-party companies, and trends suggest that this number is increasing. Even though pneumological and COVID-19 apps perform better in this metric, the sharing of PHI remains a concerning trend across the healthcare app landscape. Sensitive information, including contact details, health questionnaires, age, gender, location, device-specific identifiers, and phone numbers, is often collected by app companies and sold to media and advertising firms (Lustgarten et al., 2020), which have a strong interest in using such data to deliver targeted health-related advertisements (Iwaya et al., 2023; Neporent, 2023). Another major issue, which was not the focus of this study, is that most privacy policies are difficult to interpret without specialized legal knowledge, making informed consent even more challenging for users (Camacho et al., 2020).

Lastly, the proportion of commercially available health apps supported by efficacy or feasibility studies remains worryingly low, a concern that has been repeatedly highlighted in previous research on apps for chronic diseases and smoking cessation apps (Grundy, 2022; Sun et al., 2024). No app category, except for bipolar disorder apps, demonstrated satisfactory results regarding the availability of supporting studies. In our study, evidence was assessed as a binary measure, whether or not a supporting study existed, without evaluating the methodological quality of these studies. Should the app marketplace evolve in the right direction and a greater number of evidence-backed apps be launched, it will be worthwhile for future research to assess the quality of the supporting trials in more detail.

Our findings underscore that critical deficiencies in the app marketplace, particularly concerning data privacy and lack of empirical validation, may extend beyond mental health and are evident across various health domains. This calls for immediate action from multiple stakeholders. Policymakers and regulators should recognize that the widespread absence of evidence and responsible data handling poses significant risks and undermines the principles of evidence-based medicine. Developers must be held to higher standards to ensure that digital tools are safe, effective, and ethically designed. Our study introduces clinicians and patients to a transparent framework and accompanying database that support informed decision-making regarding health apps, aiming to help pave the way toward more trustworthy and clinically useful digital health tools.

### Limitations

There are limitations to our study. More than half of the studies identified in this systematic review used the MIND database to investigate the quality of a specific category of health apps. However, since only apps that cost less than 10 dollars or euros and adhere to certain quality standards, such as not promoting dangerous advice, are included on the database, this introduces a selection bias. As a result, it is important to acknowledge that the real-world marketplace may still differ in quality. There is also the potential of author-related bias, as many of the studies conducted on the MIND database were performed by members of the MIND team themselves. While the standardized evaluation process supports reproducibility, the overlap should be acknowledged. Moreover, some studies, such as those investigating apps for bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, identified only a small number of suitable apps for analysis. This limited sample size restricts the generalizability of findings when comparing these apps to other health app categories. To address this, we also report Cohen's h effect sizes in Table 2 to provide a complementary measure of the magnitude of group differences. It should be acknowledged that many of the apps investigated in studies using the MIND database were likely also included in the broader analyses of general mental health apps. This overlap suggests that the term “general mental health apps” has its limitations, as it does not necessarily represent a fully distinct category but rather encompasses a broad and diverse field of mental health applications, potentially influencing comparative analyses. Lastly, the dataset overall was skewed toward mental health apps, which may limit the generalizability of findings to other health domains. As such, conclusions about systemic deficiencies across the broader digital health landscape should be interpreted with caution.

## Conclusion

The results of this study highlight that the current marketplace for mental health apps, as well as apps in other medical fields, is largely lacking a strong clinical foundation and continues to raise significant privacy concerns. MIND serves as a valuable tool for identifying apps that are both effective and secure, offering tailored recommendations to clinicians and users based on their individual needs. We successfully demonstrate that MIND is not only a practical tool for facilitating app selection but also a valuable database that enables meaningful insights in comparative app quality analyses. As interest in AI and large language models now accelerates, MIND is already being used as a foundation for a new effort, mindBench.ai, given the benefits of its well-tested approach discussed in this paper.

# AI depictions of psychiatric diagnoses: a preliminary study of generative image outputs in Midjourney V.6 and DALL-E 3

**Authors:** Matthew Flathers; Griffin Smith; Ellen Wagner; Carl Erik Fisher; John Torous

**Affiliations:** 1Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Rhode Island School of Design, Providence, Rhode Island, USA | 3Harvard T H Chan School of Public Health, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Columbia University, New York, New York, USA | 5Psychiatry, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

This paper investigates how state-of-the-art generative artificial intelligence (AI) image models represent common psychiatric diagnoses. We offer key lessons derived from these representations to inform clinicians, researchers, generative AI companies, policymakers and the public about the potential impacts of AI-generated imagery on mental health discourse.

We prompted two generative AI image models, Midjourney V.6 and DALL-E 3 with isolated diagnostic terms for common mental health conditions. The resulting images were compiled and presented as examples of current AI behaviour when interpreting psychiatric terminology.

The AI models generated image outputs for most psychiatric diagnosis prompts. These images frequently reflected cultural stereotypes and historical visual tropes including gender biases and stigmatising portrayals of certain mental health conditions.

These findings illustrate three key points. First, generative AI models reflect cultural perceptions of mental disorders rather than evidence-based clinical ones. Second, AI image outputs resurface historical biases and visual archetypes. Third, the dynamic nature of these models necessitates ongoing monitoring and proactive engagement to manage evolving biases. Addressing these challenges requires a collaborative effort among clinicians, AI developers and policymakers to ensure the responsible use of these technologies in mental health contexts.

As these technologies become increasingly accessible, it is crucial for mental health professionals to understand AI’s capabilities, limitations and potential impacts. Future research should focus on quantifying these biases, assessing their effects on public perception and developing strategies to mitigate potential harm while leveraging the insights these models provide into collective understandings of mental illness.

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models including image-generation tools are becoming increasingly accessible to the public. While their impact on various fields has been studied, there is limited research on how these models specifically interpret and visually represent psychiatric concepts.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- This study provides the first thorough examination of how leading generative AI image models, Midjourney V.6 and DALL-E 3, visually interpret common psychiatric diagnoses. It reveals that these models often produce images reflecting historical visual archetypes and societal stereotypes rather than clinical realities.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- This work highlights the urgent need for collaboration between mental health professionals, AI researchers and policymakers to address the implications of AI-generated mental health imagery. It highlights current behaviours of generative models and suggests new avenues for research. The findings emphasise the importance of critical media literacy in the age of generative AI and may inform guidelines for the responsible development and use of AI tools in a mental health context.

## Introduction

The advent of generative artificial intelligence (AI) image models is rapidly reshaping our digital landscape with profound implications for the creation, dissemination and interpretation of mental health information. This transformation is significant given the well-documented impact of visual portrayals on public perceptions of mental disorders, help-seeking behaviour and stigma production.1

As generative AI tools become increasingly accessible, patients are more likely to turn to these tools for clinical information. This is particularly true in mental health fields where barriers to care often drive individuals to seek alternative sources of support. It is essential for clinicians to be cognisant of these developments. In the coming years, clinicians will likely encounter patients who have been influenced by AI-generated depictions of mental illness and a greater appreciation of how AI image models behave will enable them to proactively engage in conversations with these patients.

Research on the specific impact of AI-generated images in mental health contexts remains limited. A 2024 scoping review of generative AI in mental health identified over 30 relevant studies, yet none reported on AI-generated images.2 To address this critical gap, our paper follows a structured approach. First, we review the underlying mechanisms of AI image generation tools with a focus on text-to-image diffusion models. This technical foundation provides context for the subsequent presentation of examples showing how these models interpret and visually represent various psychiatric diagnoses. Building on these examples, we then offer key lessons for approaching these tools in a psychiatric context.

Our goal is not to condemn or promote AI image-generation tools as we acknowledge that all current generative models have inherent biases.3 Instead, we aim to meet the clear demand from clinicians for education4 about these models: What they are, how they function and how they may shape our public and personal understandings of mental health. By examining the outputs of AI models like Midjourney V.65 and DALL-E 3,6 we aim to provide mental health professionals with crucial insights into this rapidly evolving and expanding technological landscape.

## Background

The rapid evolution of generative AI technologies has significantly impacted how people access and interpret information including health-related content. Released to the public in November 2022, OpenAI’s ChatGPT reached an estimated 100 million monthly users in just 2 months.7 Preliminary research has found that, despite its recent introduction, most people are already willing to use ChatGPT for self-diagnosis8 and trust in ChatGPT’s health-related output rivals trust in Google search results on the same topics.9

While text-generation tools have been the public’s default way of engaging with AI health information to date, image-generation models are increasingly capable of serving similar functions. In October 2023, OpenAI integrated their DALL-E 3 image generation model into the paid versions of ChatGPT. Midjourney, another leader in the generative image space, has surged to 16 million users since its founding in 2022.10 Given the rapid adoption of these technologies, particularly among younger populations, there is an urgent need to study their potential impact. In this paper, we qualitatively investigate the behaviour of these generative image models as a novel method of navigating the internet’s mental health information.

We evaluated the capabilities of diffusion image models, the current state-of-the-art deep learning architecture for AI image generation. Diffusion models work by gradually adding noise to billions of images, transforming them step-by-step into visual static. This process, known as forward diffusion,11 is then reversed: The model removes the noise, reconstructing the original image in detail. Through training on vast numbers of examples, the model refines its ability to restore—and more importantly identify—essential features of images.12 This approach allows diffusion models to synthesise novel visual outputs based on text prompts.

However, it is crucial to understand the limitations and potential biases of this process. Despite their outputs’ high visual fidelity, diffusion models lack true comprehension of the content they generate. They can synthesise features in their training data but they do not possess a human-like understanding of the concepts they depict. This profound limitation demands ethical consideration, especially in sensitive domains like psychiatry.13

Furthermore, the complexity and opacity of current AI models present additional challenges. Since the most powerful models are all developed and managed by private companies, their unique processes of data sourcing, tagging and training are ‘proprietary information’. What we can responsibly infer is that most AI training data has been sourced from the internet and a large percentage of the internet has been captured by these large data sets.

Gathering internet data at this scale has several implications. First, we must assume that English is the dominant language found in the training data.14 Consequently, the biases, stigmas and psychological assumptions reflected in these models are likely influenced by perspectives prevalent in English-speaking populations.15 Second, as these data sets scale, they must source content from less curated, lower-quality sections of the internet, expanding into more chaotic, unmoderated domains. This type of growth increases an AI system’s exposure to hateful and biased inputs. Recent studies on data set scaling such as a comparative audit of LAION-400M and LAION-2B found that the prevalence of hateful content rose by nearly 12% as data set size expanded.16

This bias in data sourcing can lead to problematic representations of mental health conditions. An early example was highlighted in a 2022 Lancet Psychiatry paper where Midjourney V.2 when prompted to depict ‘schizophrenia’ produced images of horror-movie-style clowns.17 This outcome suggests that such associations persist in online discourse and by direct extension, in the training data for these generative models. In other words, it is the cultural perception of the word ‘schizophrenia’ rather than the clinical conceptualisation which is reflected in generative image models’ outputs.

The following section presents AI-generated images produced using various psychiatric diagnoses as prompts. By presenting these outputs, we aim not to endorse them but to demonstrate how AI models currently ‘perceive’ and represent psychiatric concepts. We urge readers to approach these images critically, remembering that they are algorithmic echoes of internet data, distinct from both evidence-based clinical conceptions and subjective (artistic) human interpretations. These images reflect and potentially amplify existing societal biases, stereotypes and misconceptions about psychiatric conditions. As we present these images, we invite readers to consider the ethical implications and potential consequences of such AI-generated content becoming widely accessible and disseminated. Future work examining these outputs in more detail will be necessary to move from mere demonstration to a true understanding of image model behaviour.

### Current behaviour

To understand how generative image tools portray mental disorders, we explored two of the most popular AI image generation models of 2024—Midjourney’s V.6 and OpenAI’s DALL-E 3 models. We chose these two models over other options because of their ease of use, aesthetic diversity, and popularity, all of which make them potentially impactful on general audiences rather than niche communities.

Users engage with both Midjourney and DALL-E 3 through a text-to-image interface and despite relying on the same underlying diffusion techniques, there are some notable differences in the behaviours of each tool. DALL-E 3 leverages OpenAI’s language models to make each prompt more context-aware. This allows for high-level performance at text generation in images and integration into tools like ChatGPT.6 Midjourney V.6 emphasises artistic style and creative expression through a more curated data set and a more customisable diffusion process. More so than DALL-E 3, Midjourney is designed for community collaboration through prompt sharing and Discord integration.5

Figure 1 below presents a selection of images generated by Midjourney V.6 and DALL-E 3 when prompted with isolated psychiatric diagnostic terms with no additional qualifiers. We selected these terms to highlight a diverse array of common mental health conditions listed in the WHO’s fact sheet on mental disorders.18 Exact prompt terms were chosen based on common lay terms for diagnoses (anxiety as opposed to generalised anxiety disorder, PTSD rather than post-traumatic stress disorder) to better capture the search terms likely to be used by patients when seeking mental health information online. A few exceptions were made in cases where the abbreviation was likely too noisy in the source data (OCD, DID, DPDR). For each prompt, we selected the first four successfully generated images for inclusion in figure 1. We attempted up to 10 generations before marking any result as ‘Blocked’.

If no images were returned over 10 iterations, the result is marked as Blocked with the error message included. AI, artificial intelligence; PTSD, post-traumatic stress disorder.*

## Discussion

The images above in figure 1 reveal patterns in how these AI models process and represent lay terms for psychiatric diagnoses. While we observed recurring themes, no formal consistency analysis was conducted. The patterns identified should be interpreted as qualitative insights rather than systematically validated consistencies. These patterns or biases manifest in details like the demographic choices made by Midjourney V.6 with diagnoses like borderline personality disorder, bulimia and anorexia skewing female, while autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and schizophrenia skew male.19 As well as in details like the aforementioned clown imagery resurfacing in depictions of narcissistic personality disorder across both models.

It is critical to note that these are cultural, outward-facing observations and not clinical, inward-facing understandings. The symbolic and stylistic choices in these images, though seemingly imbued with artistic meaning, are the result of complex data synthesis rather than human-like comprehension. We must ensure that patients and the public do not mistake these visual classifications of mental pathology for valid clinical information. The risk of reinforcing harmful stereotypes or misconceptions is significant, given the persuasive power of visual media.

Generative AI models acquire biases at every stage of their development—from societal prejudice in online training data, to the optimisation metrics and safety guidelines each developer puts in place. These layered biases persist even when their precise origins remain elusive. This decentralised manifestation of cultural perceptions surrounding mental illness sharply contrasts with clinical conceptualisations underscoring the gap between AI-generated imagery and evidence-based psychiatric practice. This is the first key lesson: Generative image model outputs reflect crowd-sourced, cultural perceptions of mental disorders but perceptions of disorders do not define them.

Image-based psychiatric classification (diagnosis) predates modern medicine, being evident in visual artefacts from the Middle Ages onward. As early as the Renaissance ‘the appearance of the individual is seen as a classifiable, interpretable reference to his mental state’.20 This idea gained momentum with the proliferation of engraving in the 17th and 18th centuries as early psychiatric pioneers produced images of ‘typical cases’ of mental pathology in their diagnostic classifications. The invention of photography in the latter half of the 19th century amplified these ideas further. Most famously, Jean-Martin Charcot used the early medium of photography to ‘systematically’ classify various neurological and psychiatric illnesses giving rise to the (in)famous collection of Salpêtrière photographs of hysteria.21

Each advance in image technology has initially been seen as more objective and trustworthy than its predecessors, equipping those seeking to classify diagnoses based on appearance with new tools to support their arguments. This recurring cycle of technological progress in image generation followed by misplaced trust in visual evidence, often reviving physiognomic thinking, highlights the need for vigilance as we consider the implications of AI-generated imagery for psychiatric concepts.

We must be sensitive to the misuse of visual imagery in psychiatry precisely because we so recently outgrew modes of diagnostic thinking which relied on portraying subjective images as objective medical data. In shifting away from image-based nosologies of mental illness, modern psychiatry has protected itself from a wealth of abuses which have been historically enabled by visual media and its proliferation. But the field has also failed to produce any updated ‘scientific’ or ‘objective’ images to counter these historical visual perceptions of insanity. The result is contemporary AI models which resurface outdated depictions from psychiatry’s subjective, visually-mediated past.

Figure 1 reveals several striking instances where AI-generated images align with historical visual archetypes of mental illness. Some of these outputs notably reflect the binary classifications of melancholy and mania described by Sander Gilman in his book—Seeing the Insane. He writes ‘Where melancholy is characteristically seated, with sunken head, lethargic, withdrawn, self-enclosed, the maniac is typically contorted, head and limbs thrown out, hyperactive, and exposed’.20 The frequency with which the term ‘Depression’ produced stereotypically melancholic depictions while the prompt ‘Schizophrenia’ produced maniacal ones is visual evidence of how technological advances can, perhaps inevitably, resurface historical notions. This is the second key lesson: Because generative image models are not moral agents and lack the capacity to reflect on how culture influences psychiatric understanding, it is crucial to address historically rooted bias to understand and mitigate emerging problems.

However, the landscape of AI-generated imagery is far from static. Just because a particular mode of psychiatric depiction has emerged in current models does not mean this will be a consistent feature of generative image output in the future. As these models evolve, the bias we see now will drift, making it crucial to continuously monitor and understand these changes over time. To give a sense of the change trajectory that we have already observed in generative image models, figure 2 below presents a series of images representing the evolution of Midjourney image outputs for the prompt ‘Depression’.

*Figure 2: Generative artificial intelligence image output for the prompt ‘Depression’ across Midjourney models. Version number and date of model release included under each output.*

In figure 2, we can see the outputs evolve from abstract forms into clear human likenesses in under a year. We can also observe that even models from the same company which presumably iterates on the same data sets and training processes, can show dramatic, unexpected changes between updates. This dynamic quality of generative AI further necessitates an agile approach to managing biases, one that does not solely rely on present-day moderation but prepares for tomorrow’s challenges. This brings us to the third key lesson: Generative image models are dynamic and their output is constantly changing.

Considering these key lessons, there are a few high-level (overlapping and non-exclusive) options for reducing the impact of bias in AI-generated psychiatric images. The first is to ban the models from producing any content when prompted with clinical terminology that professional medical organisations have deemed biased, stigmatising or otherwise harmful. Today, most AI developers enlist so-called ‘red teams’ to stress-test their new models for offensive output before launching them to the public.22 In this way, they identify prompts that produce violent, sexually explicit, upsetting and otherwise unacceptable content so the companies can block those keywords. Psychiatry-specific red teams could test various disorder-related terms and report on biased or disturbing results. In this way, the AI industry could work with professional medical organisations to limit the production of stigmatising psychiatric images. It is also possible, however, that blocking certain search terms in this way—as DALL-E 3 did for some psychiatric diagnostic terms in this study—could amplify stigma by suggesting that the mere depiction of certain mental health conditions is inherently dangerous, shameful or unsuitable for public viewing.

The second option is to demand that generative AI companies hire clinicians to expand on existing prompt manipulation techniques to minimise harm. Today, a user’s text prompt is often augmented by generative image tools to make the output more aesthetically pleasing, invisibly appending phrases to the input the model itself receives.23 Clinicians could help generative AI companies translate user-input prompts into safer backend prompts that have been tested and proven to produce less biased and stigmatising output results.

From a policy perspective, both approaches are unrealistic and unlikely to resolve the fundamental problems posed by generative image technologies. Both strategies rely either on top-down, specific legislative regulation or on industry self-regulation, both of which are unlikely to occur for such a niche concern within a heterogeneous, globally dispersed and rapidly developing AI marketplace. It is also unlikely that professional organisations such as the American Psychiatric Association would be able to take on this responsibility.

From a consumer perspective, users will simply change their search terms to circumvent language-based prompt guardrails. We see this type of behaviour modification repeatedly across the internet.24 As an example, when social media platforms like TikTok and Facebook attempted to remove suicide-related content, users quickly engaged in what is colloquially called ‘Algospeak’, shifting to the use of terms like ‘unalive’ and ‘$u1c1d3’ instead of ‘suicide’ to avoid many of the guardrails that social media companies attempted to implement.25

The third and more realistic route forward is to isolate the specific biases that exist in AI image models today and better identify their root causes. By doing so, we open a novel window into the complex network of language and imagery surrounding mental disorders. This unique perspective can, in turn, help us begin to reduce the overall risk of harm to patients and the public posed by advancements in generative technologies. Thus, rather than simply reiterate the presence of bias, we seek to frame the cultural stigmas surfaced by these AI models as valuable data for scientific psychiatric inquiry. By studying specific biases, we may uncover insights that can inform clinical practice.

It is critical that patients and providers recognise that the images produced by these tools are aesthetic profiles of diagnostic categories, not clinical ones. This distinction is vital to ensuring that the therapeutic space remains grounded in human expertise. Consequently, AI research should shift from a reactionary model of censorship and invisible prompt engineering to proactive collaboration between researchers, clinicians, professional organisations, tech companies and those with lived experience. Such collaborations can inform how the many stakeholders listed above participate in the evolution of next-generation AI tools to foster a more targeted and ethically aware approach.

### Future directions

As we confront the reality of generative technologies, our focus must shift from attempting to halt their proliferation to striving for a practical understanding of their behaviour. The goal is not to achieve perfect, unbiased models—such an aspiration is unattainable—but to generate valuable human insight from divergent digital interpretations of mental illness. By analysing how AI systems represent psychiatric concepts, we gain new perspectives on how these conditions are (mis)understood in our broader culture.

From this introduction, several complementary—though non-exhaustive—avenues for future research and discussion emerge:

- Productive image model behaviour: Meaningful progress toward better visual representations of psychiatric disorders in image model output will require extensive collaboration between all mental health stakeholders. Defining what would be a ‘better’ representation is complex and subjective; however, we suggest it should at a minimum avoid harm, minimise stigma and otherwise be in reasonable alignment with scientific and professional clinical judgement.

- Mental health literacy: Further research assessing patient and clinician reactions to generative images produced from psychiatric concept prompts would be valuable to better understand the likely impact of these tools on mental health literacy. The need for more in-depth studies in this area is supported by recent work from Nutbeam.26

- Human-computer interaction (HCI): Further research is needed to explore the role of HCI in developing and testing AI models for psychiatry as well as in designing tools based on these models. Investigations into how users—clinicians, patients and developers—interact with such systems are key to ensuring tools in the space are usable, effective and ethical. The need for this research is supported by recent work from Yang and Yang27 and De Choudhury et al.28

- Computational aesthetics: Deeper quantitative research into the qualities of generative image output for psychiatric terminology would be valuable to assess if the qualitative results uncovered here are observed at scale. The importance of aesthetics in social science research is well-established and new tools are being developed to make this form of research more approachable.29

- Cross-cultural comparisons: The issue of translation in psychiatry is complex and cultural contexts greatly affect the way people interpret symptoms and conceptualise their experiences.30 Testing how generative models respond to psychiatric diagnosis prompts in different languages is critical to perform alongside English testing as there is every likelihood that observed behaviours, biases and risks associated with these tools will differ between languages and cultures.

Insights gained from these lines of inquiry would: (1) contribute to an enhanced understanding of the rapidly evolving opportunities and challenges presented by generative AI, (2) inform approaches to mitigate potential harms associated with generative image models, (3) ensure the design of tools that are useful and usable—and maximise benefits of such technology for diverse populations and (4) pave the way for responsible integration of AI technologies in mental health research and practice.

## Conclusion

Generative AI models while increasingly integrated into daily internet use are far from reliable facilitators of clinical information. They reflect current perceptions, historical inaccuracies and linguistic biases—a combination that can shape public understanding of psychiatric conditions. This exploration of the capabilities and outputs of Midjourney V.6 and DALL-E 3 underscores the importance of viewing these outputs as subjective representations. As generative AI improves, it is crucial for everyone—clinicians, researchers, developers and the public—to remember that the images produced are decentralised interpretations, not clinical portrayals. However, it is equally important to recognise that these subjective, crowd-sourced interpretations offer a unique window into collective perceptions of mental disorders, providing valuable data for scientific inquiry and potential pathways for addressing stigma and misinformation in the field of psychiatry.
